question: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

The IMEC corridor is a strategically important connectivity project, supported by the European Union, the United States, India, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, with the aim of strengthening trade, energy and transport networks between Europe, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific1. However, according to recent official statements by Turkish and Saudi Arabian government officials, the two countries plan to develop a rail link in competition with IMEC2, creating new data regarding the strategic architecture of connectivity corridors in the wider region. Given that IMEC has been presented as a project of high geoeconomic and geopolitical importance for European competitiveness, energy security and the diversification of trade routes: 1.
Does the Commission still consider IMEC strategically and economically viable in light of the Ankara-Riyadh initiative?
How does the Commission assess the participation of candidate countries, such as Türkiye, in projects competing with initiatives supported by the European Union and its strategic partners?

What specific measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure the implementation and geoeconomic effectiveness of IMEC, as well as to strengthen the Member States that are investing in this strategic route and expect significant economic, energy and geopolitical benefits from its operation?

https://global-gateway-forum.ec.europa.eu/news/global-gateway-forum-accelerating-digitaltransformation-through-imec-eu-africa-india-digital-2025-10-10_en. 2 https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/turkey-saudi-arabia-aim-build-rail-link-with-jordan-syriaminister-says-2026-06-14/. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The Commission considers the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) a strategically important initiative. Its core objective is to strengthen connectivity between Europe, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific, and support resilient, efficient and sustainable links in the areas of transport, energy and digital infrastructure. Recent events, notably the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, have made IMEC more relevant than ever, reinforcing the need for diversified supply routes. This is fully acknowledged by IMEC signatories who regularly meet at senior officials’ level. The Commission, alongside other IMEC signatories, considers IMEC to be a ‘network of corridors’ which can extend beyond the initial route envisaged in the Memorandum of Understanding. In this context, IMEC is envisaged as a broader and more flexible network. The EU sees IMEC as part of a set of diverse but interconnected initiatives that improve connectivity between Europe, the Middle East and India, promoting inclusiveness, complementarity and flexibility rather than competition. This applies to the Ankara–Riyadh initiative and to other routes under development in the region. The Commission will continue to work with IMEC signatories and relevant stakeholders to advance viable projects and collectively support the broader objective of diversified, resilient and efficient connectivity, therefore maximising the geoeconomic effectiveness of IMEC.
